newsitem.title: UK: UK government hesitates on press vs privacy issue.
newsitem.headline: UK government hesitates on press vs privacy issue.

text.p: A British cabinet minister, reacting to a furore over the media's pursuit of the royal family, said on Thursday she would be reluctant to bring in legislation covering the invasion of privacy.

National Heritage Secretary Virginia Bottomley was speaking after the head of Britain's press watchdog chided newspapers for a spate of reports about the royal family and warned editors they were undermining their right to self-regulation.
The best-selling Sun newspaper had to apologise to Princess Diana on Wednesday after it used photographs from a hoax video apparently showing her with a former lover.
Bottomley told journalists at the annual conference of the ruling Conservative Party in Bournemouth there was a danger that a privacy law could backfire.

"Those who wished to have their privacy defended could find their private lives made public by cross-examination in court," she said. Media affairs are part of Bottomley's ministerial responsibilities.
"This is an issue which will remain under review. It is a subject on which there is very strong feeling. I think Lord Wakeham is being extremely wise in issuing a warning shot today."

In a letter in Thursday's Times, Lord Wakeham, chairman of the Press Complaints Commission, said the newspaper industry's self-regulation system was "in danger of being undermined" by stories about peoples' private lives.
He said he had been disturbed by recent events.

"Although these events concern primarily members and former members of the royal family, the key issues they raise -- invasion of privacy and the use of public interest defence by newspapers -- have wider ramifications," he said.

"Nobody would benefit from statutory controls...I therefore trust all those who have an interest in these issues will cooperate with me and with the commission as we chart the way forward in strengthening self-regulation."

The threat of privacy legislation has been raised repeatedly in Britain, usually following media revelations about the royal family. Despite a warning from one of Bottomley's predecessors in 1989 that the press was "drinking in the last chance saloon", Prime Minister John Major has yet to consider legislation.
Royal supporters have placed much of the blame for the breakdown of the marriage of Princess Diana and Prince Charles on the media, which revelled in their marital troubles.
Diana's former sister-in-law the Duchess of York, better known as Fergie, has also suffered a barrage of press reports about her extra-marital affairs and financial troubles.
Wakeham said he was particularly concerned about media pressure on children of the royal family.

This week the Daily Express had a front-page report on the alleged first love of William, 14-year-old son of Diana and Charles. Buckingham Palace demanded an apology and it transpired the pair had never met.
"When a story breaks they (the children) are the first to suffer," Wakeham wrote. When William went to Eton private school, editors agreed to Wakeham's request to leave him alone.
